abstract: Indeed Hiring Lab analysis (Sept 17, 2026) of millions of US job postings with an advertised annual salary, sorting occupations into terciles by Indeed's GenAI Skill Transformation Index. Since 2021, advertised pay in the most AI-exposed occupations rose about 46% versus 25% in the least-exposed; the two groups tracked closely for a year after ChatGPT, and the gap widened from around 2024. A difference-in-differences with month fixed effects finds a post-ChatGPT advertised-pay premium for exposed occupations of 5.7% (occupation FE), 4.7% (job-title FE) and 2.4% (occupation-by-seniority FE, not significant at 5%). The cumulative gap rises with seniority (about 17 points senior, 12 mid, 2 entry), but measured against a 2022 baseline it is far more even (roughly 5, 6 and 7 points). Part of the rise reflects a shift toward fewer, more senior postings: in the most-exposed occupations the entry-level share of salaried postings fell from 29% to 10% between 2021 and 2026 and the senior share rose from 22% to 47%. Indeed reads the pattern as AI acting more as a complement to skilled workers than a replacement.
keyFindings: Advertised pay in the most AI-exposed occupations rose about 46% since 2021, vs 25% in the least-exposed.

Post-ChatGPT advertised-pay premium for exposed occupations: 5.7% with occupation fixed effects, 4.7% within job title, 2.4% holding seniority mix constant within occupation (the last not significant at 5%).
Cumulative gap since 2021: about 17 points for senior postings (45% vs 28% growth), about 12 for mid-level, 2 for entry-level.
Against a 2022 baseline the post-ChatGPT gap is roughly 5 points at entry, 6 at mid and 7 at senior.
Entry-level share of salaried postings in the most-exposed occupations fell from 29% to 10% (2021–2026); senior share rose from 22% to 47%; the least-exposed tilt was about a third as large.
methodology: Difference-in-differences on Indeed US job postings that state an annual salary, 2021–2026. Exposure: Indeed GenAI Skill Transformation Index (share of a role's ~2,900 skills judged open to 'hybrid' or 'full' GenAI transformation), occupations cut into equal-count terciles; headline compares top vs bottom tercile. Occupation shares fixed at 2021 averages. Fixed effects for occupation (or job title, or occupation × seniority) and month; standard errors clustered by occupation. Seniority from the entry/mid/senior tag on each posting.
qualifiers: Tier 2: industry research from a job-postings platform, unrefereed. Advertised pay is the offer price on posted jobs, not realized earnings, and the sample of salaried postings skews senior (senior share ~37% vs ~14% of all US postings). Some of the premium reflects composition — fewer, more senior postings in exposed occupations — which is why the premium falls to an insignificant 2.4% when seniority mix is held constant; Indeed argues that control may over-correct because AI may be driving the seniority tilt. The seniority split is described by the authors as suggestive; most regression terms behind it are not statistically significant. Exposure is an AI-capability index, not observed adoption. The exposed group is concentrated in knowledge-work sectors whose postings also rebounded over the past year, so sectoral dynamics are not fully separated from AI.
